old: Its spread across languages seems to trace the same route this animal took out of the Near East, especially after it found fame in Egypt some 4,000 years ago.
Scholars suspect the English word ultimately comes from an Afroasiatic source, though every candidate word proposed so far runs into trouble.
It shares a root with Spanish and Portuguese 'gato,' and with words like French 'chat' and German 'Katze.'
clues: This household pet's name possibly began in an Afroasiatic language, and the animal itself was especially popular in Egypt around 4000 years ago.
Not a kitten but the grown animal: a whiskered, purring pet that hunts mice and grooms itself. Old English had separate forms for the male and the female.
Its relatives include Spanish gato, French chat and German Katze, and it is the animal said to have nine lives or to have gotten your tongue.
